zugeo

DuckDB, GDAL and the Python geospatial stack hand geometries around as GeoArrow columns and store them as GeoParquet. In R they usually become sf objects on the way in: one R object per geometry, a coordinate reference system resolved through PROJ, and digits that depend on who printed the text.

zugeo keeps a geometry column as what it is, Arrow memory with its CRS and edge type, and works on it there.

  • Geometries stay in Arrow memory. A geo_vctr holds positions into the arrays it was read in, so subsetting and sorting copy no coordinates. With zugeo loaded, zuarrow reads and writes every GeoArrow type as one.
  • Exact or an error. WKB, WKT and the native layouts convert with every coordinate intact: WKT prints the shortest digits that read back to the same double. A conversion that would lose an edge type is an error unless you ask for it.
  • A CRS is carried, never guessed. zugeo stores a CRS as it was given and compares it without PROJ; it never resolves a code to a definition.
  • Kernels over the buffers. Bounding boxes, Hilbert keys and spatial sorting run over the coordinates without an R object per geometry, and the packed R-tree and k-d tree indexes are byte for byte those of flatbush and kdbush.
  • GeoParquet 2.0 and 1.1, with the qio package: native GEOMETRY types, row groups skipped by box, and a validator that reports what gpq validate does.

zugeo has no system requirements: it bundles geoarrow-c, and imports only zuarrow and zujson.

Installation

zugeo is not on CRAN yet. Install the development version from GitHub:

# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("pedrobtz/zugeo")

Usage 

library(zugeo)

A geo_vctr reads WKT or WKB and keeps the CRS beside the geometries.

cities <- geo_vctr(
  c("POINT (-9.139 38.722)", "POINT (-8.611 41.150)", "POINT (2.352 48.857)"),
  crs = "OGC:CRS84"
)
cities
#> <geo_vctr[3] geoarrow.wkt wkt; crs authority_code; edges planar>
#> [1] POINT (-9.139 38.722)
#> [2] POINT (-8.611 41.150)
#> [3] POINT (2.352 48.857)

Coordinates come back exactly as they went in, through any encoding.

x <- geo_points(0.1 + 0.2, 1 / 3)
cat(geo_as_wkt(x))
#> POINT (0.30000000000000004 0.3333333333333333)
identical(geo_coords(geo_vctr(geo_as_wkb(x)))$x, 0.1 + 0.2)
#> [1] TRUE

An R-tree finds what intersects a box. Its bytes are in flatbush’s format, magic byte fb first, so flatbush in JavaScript and geo-index in Rust and Python load them unchanged.

tree <- geo_rtree(cities)
geo_query_box(tree, geo_extent(-10, 38, -8, 42, crs = "OGC:CRS84"))
#> [1] 1 2
geo_index_raw(tree)[1:2]
#> [1] fb 38

Lines on the sphere have no planar box, so asking for one is an error.

route <- geo_vctr("LINESTRING (-9.139 38.722, 2.352 48.857)",
  crs = "OGC:CRS84", edges = "spherical"
)
geo_box(route)
#> Error in `geo_box()`:
#> ! A planar box can be wrong for "spherical" edges, which may bulge past their vertices or cross the antimeridian. Pass `lossy = "warn"` or `"allow"` for the planar box anyway.

With qio installed, a data frame of geometries becomes GeoParquet. Reading with bbox skips the row groups whose statistics miss the box, then keeps the rows that meet it.

path <- tempfile(fileext = ".parquet")
df <- data.frame(name = c("Lisbon", "Porto", "Paris"))
df$geometry <- cities
geo_write_parquet(df, path)
geo_read_parquet(path, bbox = c(-10, 38, -8, 42))
#>     name              geometry
#> 1 Lisbon POINT (-9.139 38.722)
#> 2  Porto  POINT (-8.611 41.15)

Every function is prefixed geo_, apart from zugeo_info(). zugeo’s errors inherit from zugeo_error, with a class for each kind, such as zugeo_edges_error and zugeo_crs_error.

Related work

zugeo implements the GeoArrow 0.2 and GeoParquet specifications over the bundled geoarrow-c and nanoarrow libraries. It is tested on the geoarrow-data corpus and, in CI, against DuckDB, GDAL, sf, geos, s2, wk, gpq, flatbush, kdbush and geo-index, and loads beside the geoarrow and nanoarrow packages.
